title: LEO II - The Hometown Cut
claimCheck: Every spoken figure measured; see the CLAIM CHECK section of LEO2-SCRIPT.md
transcript:
Hey. I'm Leo.

I'm an artificial intelligence, speaking in David Thomas's voice, cloned with his blessing.

Before I say anything else, I want to tell you the rule I run under.

Every number I am about to say was measured before I was allowed to say it.

Where we have not measured, I will tell you that instead. Out loud. In the middle of my own pitch.

That is not modesty. That is the product.

Let me start at home.

Sacramento. A brain MRI. Procedure code seven zero five five three.

The middle of this market is five hundred ninety one dollars and ninety seven cents.

The top of this market is fifteen hundred thirty five dollars and forty nine cents.

Twenty two thousand two hundred and thirty two filings behind those two numbers. Filed in July.

I am going to say the sample size and the filing date every single time I say a price.

That habit is the whole company.

Here is what changed, and why this is possible at all.

Federal rules now require health plans and hospitals to publish what they actually pay.

Not a range. Not an average. The negotiated dollar amount, provider by provider.

The rule says those files must be available to any person, free of charge, with no account and no password.

Any person. That includes you.

Almost nobody on the buying side has ever opened one, because a single file can be larger than everything you have ever downloaded, combined.

We read them. That is the entire trick. There is no magic here. There is just the reading.

Now. Yesterday, on the call planning this afternoon, you asked us three questions. Let me answer all three, honestly.

You asked about pharmacy. About rebates. About pass through.

Here is the honest answer, and it is not the one a vendor usually gives you.

The rebate is a contract secret. No public file holds it.

The federal government does collect it. It collects aggregate rebates, pass through, and spread pricing from every plan sponsor.

And the government's own website says, in writing, that it cannot make that information publicly available.

So if someone sells you rebate visibility built from public data, ask them for their sample size. Then watch what happens.

But there is a door nobody is walking through.

The drugs administered in a clinic. The infusions. The injections. The ones billed to the medical benefit and not the pharmacy benefit.

Those are negotiated rates. Negotiated rates are public now.

They never touch a pharmacy benefit manager, so no rebate contract hides them.

They are in our system tonight, priced against the federal payment limit, employer group by employer group.

You asked whether you can see one network against another, corner to corner.

Yes. Same procedure, same city, two carriers, side by side, per code, each with its own sample size and its own filing date.

You asked the biggest one. Whether a self funded plan could design its own network from this.

Here is my answer, and I want to be careful, because the careful version is the useful one.

The prices exist. Provider by provider. We hold them.

Nobody who has ever built a network has started with the full price map in their hands.

But we do not sign contracts and we do not run a plan. We measure. You and your administrator design.

I will never pretend that line is blurry, because the day it blurs is the day I become something you cannot trust.

Now let me show you the part that makes people quiet.

It is late August. Your renewals are on your desk.

In this county alone, one hundred ninety eight employers fund their own health plans.

We know that because they said so, on a federal form, with their own names on it.

Two hundred and one thousand four hundred and one people are covered inside those plans.

One hundred ninety two of those employers name the agency that already holds the account.

That is not a lead list somebody sold us. That is public filing, read carefully, by us.

And when their carrier quotes a trend number this fall, here is the comparator nobody hands them.

Across California's fully insured large group filings, the median approved increase was four point three percent.

One hundred seventy six filings. Thirty eight carriers. Filed with the state.

Your client will be quoted a number. Now you know what the state actually approved.

And one more, for a Kaiser town.

Everyone says Kaiser is invisible. That its prices cannot be seen.

I want to be precise, because precise is the point. I have not seen a transparency product that prices Kaiser.

But Kaiser Roseville publishes a file. Two hundred and fifteen megabytes of it. Version three point zero point one. Dated April first. Attested true, by a named human being, under Kaiser's own hospital number.

Nobody opened it. We did.

Now here is the part I insist on.

Ask me what the arbitration multiple is for Sacramento specifically.

I will refuse you.

Not because it is hidden. Because our sample here is too thin to defend, and this company does not hand you a number it cannot defend.

Not even in its own hometown. Especially not in its own hometown.

The facility half of that site of care spread I showed you is the national federal amount, not wage adjusted to this metro. So the direction and the size of that gap are right, and the facility half is not local. I am telling you that rather than letting you find it.

Below a hundred filings, we show you the refusal instead of the number.

The first bad number you hand a chief financial officer is the last one they ever trust.

So we would rather be the company that shows you its own edges.

Here is where this goes.

We are building toward the day every market in this country is lit the way this one is lit tonight.

Every code. Every carrier. Readable by the people whose money it actually is.

That money is not the carrier's. It is not ours. In a self funded plan it belongs to the employer and to the people who work there.

The plans could always read their own numbers.

This is the year the other side of the table learns to read.

And it starts at home.

Come find us. Ask for the knee.

And ask us to name the hundred and ninety eight.
